Hi, Mirela! So, you’re thinking about living in New York one day?
Well, it’s a dream for now. But if I lived there, I’d want a quiet neighborhood close to the city.
Then I’d look at Brooklyn. It’s lively, but some streets are really calm.
And how much is the rent there? Could I afford a two-bedroom?
A two-bedroom is about four thousand a month. A studio apartment is cheaper, around twenty-eight hundred.
Wow. The cost of living is really high. What about the commute to Manhattan?
By subway, twenty-five minutes. Honestly, if I were you, I’d come for a month first and see how it feels.
That’s a good idea. If I did that, I’d know if I could really settle in.

I was born in Queens, and I've lived in New York all my life. People always ask me how anyone can afford it. Honestly, it's hard. Almost half of my salary goes to the rent, and I live in a small apartment. I don't have a car. Parking is crazy expensive, and the subway goes everywhere anyway. So why do I stay? Because there's always something to do. A free concert in the park, a new restaurant, a museum I haven't seen. If I moved to a smaller city, I'd have more space and more money. But I'd miss the energy. I know I would.

When my company sent me to New York, I was so excited. And then, for the first three months, I was terribly homesick. I missed my family, I missed the quiet streets of my little town, and everything in Manhattan felt too fast and too loud. What helped me settle in was a running group in my neighborhood. Every Saturday morning, we ran along the river and then had coffee together. Slowly, those people became my friends. So if I were you, and you wanted to move abroad, I'd say this: find one activity you love, and do it in the new city from the very first week.

I work in Manhattan, but I live in New Jersey, with my wife and two kids. My commute is about an hour each way, by train. People think that's terrible. But if we lived in Manhattan, we couldn't afford a big apartment, and the kids wouldn't have a garden. So for us, it makes sense. And I've learned to use the time. In the morning, I read the news or listen to a podcast. In the evening, I sometimes just close my eyes and rest. If I drove, I couldn't do any of that. Actually, the train is the only time of the day when nobody needs me.
